Q: How to disable the error overlay (red bar) in Nuxt 2 when receiving bad responses from backend? A:

You can customise the loading progress bar in Nuxt.

In your case, try setting loading.failedColor to transparent.

You can also disable the loading in general.

Since your using axios plugin, you can also intercept errors with such codes and handle them in a custom way using $axios.onError.

Q: Is there any documentation for xmlseclibs? A:

To solve the prefix problem, simply pass an empty string to the XMLSecurityDSig constructor:

$dsig = new XMLSecurityDSig('');

If you don't pass the prefix parameter in the constructor at all, it will use the default value, which is 'ds'.

Q: "serializable" transactions vs Guarded atomic UPDATE, concurrency racing conditions A:

My "concurent system" became a lot more robust when I started passing around "requests" (for resources); instead of (indirectly) maintaining state by passing a lot of "parameters" around. My single request class (with interfaces for specific requests) includes a "toolbox" of a Stopwatch, logger, and background worker reference for progress reporting on each request (each request spawns a background worker that "completes" with a UI update and does intermediate % progress control updates). Concurrent queues manage the submission, deleting of redundant requests ("UI flooding"), and dispatching.

Q: Why does Python attempt item assignment after in-place += on a mutable element inside a tuple? A:

Thats not the same, you could try with the int:

t = (1, 2, [30, 40])


second = t[1]
second += 1
print(t) # (1, 2, [30, 40])

while:

t = (1, 2, [30, 40])

t[1] += 1 # fails

This is the same operation for the int and the list, and the interpreter don't know what kind of object this is, so can't assign the new object to the tuple. It could check if the id changed, but I don't think that would be useful in the real life

Q: Finding k-largest elements of a very large file (while k is very LARGE) A:

An O(n) solution is to split the file recursively, recording the size A and B of entries in the "Above" file and the "Below" file, respectively, as well as their minimum and maximum values. If k < B, split the Below file at (min + max) / 2 and look for the (k-A)-th largest element; if A < k, split the Above file instead and look for the k-th largest element. The k elements you are looking for are contained in the set of files with minimum element larger than the value of the k-th largest element. Of course, when the split files are small enough to fit in memory, you can finish the process in memory. Since N = sum(i = 1 .. log_2(N): N / 2^i), this is O(N).

If the constant is too high for that method, then make a histogram with R bins instead, and find which bin contains the k-th highest value. Filter for just the entries in that bin (O(N)). Repeat this process until the bin is small enough to fit in memory (at most O(log_R(N)) times), and finish finding the k-th largest entry in memory. Then make a final pass, filtering only for all the entries greater than the k-th largest. Since R >> 2, we note that sum(i = 1 .. log_R(N): N / R^i) < N and this algorithm is also O(N), but will require passes through a smaller number of entries.
